slides.title: Purpose and stages
bullets: Quality control (internal control) in clinical diagnostic laboratories is carried out every day, in every analytical series.
Pre-analytical stage: preparing the patient, collecting the material, registration, primary handling of the specimen, delivery to the laboratory and storage until the test.
Analytical stage: that the method was chosen correctly, material and reagents were dosed correctly, and the reaction, measurement and calculation were done correctly.
Final stage: that forms are filled in correctly, the results are evaluated and the conditions for reaching the treating physician.

slides.title: Control material
bullets: The basis of internal control is the daily, long-term use of standardised control material.
The point is to test one control material periodically and record the results on a control chart.
Control materials made at plants authorised for use in Uzbekistan are recommended; if that is not possible, control material made from leftovers of unused specimens (serum, plasma, urine) is used.
For haematology control: stabilised blood, special suspensions for checking cell counts, haemolysates, fixed blood smears.

slides.title: Rules for using control material
bullets: 1. Before use study the supplied instructions (the passport) carefully.
2. Even if the instructions say that the material is free of hepatitis and HIV antigens, handle it with great care.
3. To prepare for work use the instructions recommended by the manufacturer.
4. Open the vial very carefully so as not to spill; measure the solvent exactly.
5. After the vial is tightly closed mix it well without foaming and observe the dissolving time.

slides.title: Factors affecting the quality of biochemical tests
rows: Water clean with pH 6.5–7.5; in doubt water from another source; reagent bottle caps clean
Pipette fits the volume and is sound; correct order of work, temperature, incubation time and dosing
Solvent volume, shelf life, storage rules (storing above 37 °C sharply reduces stability)
Solvent volume, pipette, water quality, shelf life, stability at 2–6 °C

Quality of collection; centrifuge speed and temperature; separating plasma/serum from cells; closing containers; plastic containers only; freezing a specimen kept longer than 4 hours; not testing turbid, haemolysed, lipaemic or very high-bilirubin specimens
Calibration, programme parameters, not working in scratched cuvettes, wiping the optical system

slides.title: Pre-analytical factors
bullets: Biological factors: sex, age, ethnicity, physiological state (exercise, pregnancy), biological rhythms; diet, fasting, body position, physical activity, smoking, alcohol.
Iatrogenic factors: diagnostic procedures, operations, treatment procedures, taking drugs.
Conditions of collection: time of collection, preparing the body site, cleanliness of containers, primary handling (centrifugation and so on), storage time and dispatch.

Blood: outpatients in the morning between 8 and 10, inpatients after waking or between 7 and 9; fasting or after a light breakfast, lying or sitting; not recommended after physiotherapy, X-ray or physical exertion.
Errors in registering the patient and the biomaterial also affect the result.

slides.title: Errors in the analytical and final stages
bullets: Errors in the analytical stage: not keeping the temperature regime, inexact measuring of sample and reagent, instrument faults and programme changes.
Also low staff qualification, carelessness, mistakes in calculation, and inaccuracies in preparing reagents.
Final control: the analytical validity of the result is checked; agreement with the passport part of the request; comparison with earlier or parallel results of the same patient.
If the difference between results is large it is discussed with the clinicians and the test is repeated if needed.
There is a table of critical results that call for urgent action; it is important to state the time the result was sent on the form.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Treat control material as potentially hazardous even when it is stated to be free of hepatitis and HIV antigens.
When opening and mixing the vial avoid spills and splashes; wear gloves.
Used vials and instruments are disinfected.
